question.leadin: Name these Anglo-Saxon kings with distinctive epithets No regnal numbers are required.
question.text: One king of this name, the son of Aethelred, was called "the Confessor" and was the last king of the House of Wessex. Another king of this name was known as "Longshanks" and "Hammer of the Scots" when he fought William Wallace.
question.answerHtml: Edward [or Edward the Confessor; or Edward Longshanks; or Edward, Hammer of the Scots; or Edward I; or The Lord Edward]
question.clue: A third man of this name was supported by the English victory at the Battle of Halidon Hill, which was not enough to overcome his rival David II's claim to the throne.

swap.text: During the Third Crusade, English forces were led by the first English king of this name, nicknamed "the Lionheart." The third English king of this name supposedly murdered the "Princes in the Tower."
swap.clue: The second king of this name was the last Plantagenet monarch and was deposed by Henry IV.

question.leadin: Answer the following questions about World War I.
question.text: This biggest naval battle of World War I saw Sir John Jellicoe lead the British to a tactical victory over Germany and deliver a crushing blow to any hopes of Germany gaining naval superiority over the Allies.
question.clue: The ironically named (+) Invincible was sunk during this battle, which included a phase called the Run to the South.

swap.leadin: Name these Prime Ministers of the United Kingdom.
swap.text: This Prime Minister of the UK leads a coalition government with Liberal Democrat Nick Clegg. At 43, he's the youngest Prime Minister in about 200 years.
swap.clue: In August 2011, this leader controversially proposed that social media might be restricted during riots, such as the ones which swept his capital earlier that month.

question.text: The Jacobites became active after this event, in which James II was overthrown due to his Catholic sympathies. The English Bill of Rights was adopted in the wake of this event.
question.clue: This event was partially triggered by a letter sent by the "Immortal Seven".

swap.leadin: Early English monarchs are often forgotten.
swap.text: This only king of England to hold the title of "the Great" was a king of Wessex.
swap.clue: This leader retreated to his childhood hunting location, the Somerset marshes, following a defeat at Chippenham, but then regrouped and won the Battle of Edington.

question.leadin: The politician previously served as Chancellor of the Exchequer under Lord Derby.
question.text: Name this only British Prime Minister of Jewish descent, who bestowed the title Empress of India on Queen Victoria.
question.clue: He drafted legislation giving the vote to every adult male houseowner living in a borough, the Second Reform Act.

swap.leadin: Answer these questions about Jews in England.
swap.text: Benjamin Disraeli, the first Prime Minister of Jewish ancestry, served this nineteenth-century queen, as did his rival William Gladstone. She ruled for sixty-three years.
swap.clue: One of this monarch's mentors was Lord Melbourne, and Robert Peel took power under this ruler.

question.leadin: Henry IV issued De Heretico Comburendo to combat these people, who were sometimes also called Beghards.
question.text: Name these English religious dissenters whose leader, John Wyclif, advocated such reforms as translating the Bible into English.
question.clue: They launched a short-lived open rebellion after William Fisher helped organize them at St. Giles Fields, which would have been led by a man who inspired the depiction of Falstaff, John Oldcastle.

swap.text: The family name refers to the red shield on the house where the ancestors of this famous family lived. For fifteen points, name this family dynasty founded by Mayer whose sons Amschel, Nathan, Jacob, Solomon, and Karl established a system of banks across Europe in the 1800's.
swap.clue: Legendarily, one member of this family heard about the result of the Battle of Waterloo through a carrier pigeon, which was also how they supposedly gained advance knowledge of financial events.

question.leadin: Answer these questions about a British politician.
question.text: is considered the first British prime minister, a position he began to hold during this monarch's reign.

swap.leadin: Originating in a meeting between Leon Gambetta and the then-Prince of Wales in 1881, it was finally put into place two decades later by Theophile Delcasse and Lord Lansdowne.
swap.text: Name this "friendly concord" between England and France which took effect in 1904.
swap.clue: Articles 6 and 7 ensured the free passage of the Suez Canal and Strait of Gibraltar, while Article 4 stipulated that no customs duties were to be imposed in Morocco and Egypt.

question.leadin: Weavers angry at the creator of this invention broke into his house in Oswaldtwistle, forcing him to flee.
question.text: Name this invention created by James Hargreaves, expanding on the flying shuttle of John Kay. One worker could process eight spools at once with the first version of this invention, which led to factory production with cotton.
question.clue: Despite them being destroyed in the first two villages they were built in, by 1788 there were over 20,000 of them throughout the country.

swap.leadin: This man persisted with using Manchurian ponies instead of stronger light or dark ones, but they all ended up dying anyway.
swap.text: Name this man who ended his diary with the line "For God's sake look after our people." This man also wrote in his diary that Lawrence Oates marched to his death after saying "I am just going outside and may be some time."
swap.clue: While leading an Antarctic expedition, Hillary set up a base named for this explorer, who led the Terra Nova expedition to the South Pole. Before his death, he wrote a diary entry stating "For God's sake look after our people".

question.leadin: Robert Walpole's brother-in-law Charles Townshend ("TOWN-zuhnd") was nicknamed after this crop due to his constant advocacy for it.
question.text: Name this fodder crop that was grown in a four-year cycle along with wheat, barley and clover in the Norfolk four-course system.

swap.leadin: Answer the following about developments in the advertisement industry in the early 20th century.
swap.text: As part of an ad campaign for a product named after this man, Gerald Lambert revived the word "halitosis."This man pioneered the use of carbolic acid to sterilize equipment as part of his work in antiseptic surgery.
swap.answerHtml: Joseph Lister [or Joseph Lister, Baron Lister of Lyme Regis; accept Listerine]
swap.clue: A more successful advocate of antiseptic surgery was this British surgeon, who built on the ideas of Louis Pasteur. A consumer product named for this man popularized the concept of "chronic halitosis."

question.leadin: Answer these questions about British kings possibly killed by crossbows.
question.text: Geoffrey Gaimer reports that this king was killed in a crossbow attack. This monarch led a 1016 uprising against his father Æthelred the Unready and was succeeded by his rival Cnut the Great.
question.clue: By marrying Ealdgyth he gained claim to the Five Burroughs, and this ruler opposed his father's advisor Edric Streona.

swap.leadin: Name these things about the executions ordered by Mary Tudor.
swap.text: Before he was burned at the stake he remarked, "We shall this day light such a candle in England as I trust shall never be put out." This Protestant preacher had already been imprisoned in the Tower of London for his earlier opposition to Henry's Six Articles.

question.text: Sands was held in this prison during his hunger strike, during which he was elected to parliament as a member of its anti-H block group. Liam Averill escaped from here by dressing up as a woman during a Christmas party.

swap.leadin: It was planned by the namesake Italian banker for religious reasons, but it was exposed in 1571 before it could enthrone Mary, Queen of Scots.
swap.text: Name this abortive conspiracy against Elizabeth I.
swap.clue: The Flemish agent Charles Baillie was arrested at Dover and eventually testified the truth behind letters written by the Bishop of Ross, a primary planner of this event.
